# The Linux system {#sec-linux-system}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Read a permission string such as `-rw-r--r--` or `drwxr-x---`, say
   who may read, change, or enter, and change it with `chmod`.
2. Make a script run as a command with a shebang line and the
   executable bit, and explain `Permission denied` and `command not
   found` when it does not.
3. Explain how the shell finds a command through `PATH`, find which
   copy runs with `type -a`, and set environment variables for one
   command, one session, or every new terminal.
4. Find, stop, and end your own processes with {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}},
   `ps`, `top`, and `kill`, and find what is filling a disk with `df`
   and `du`.
5. Recognise when a command depends on GNU (Linux) or BSD (macOS)
   tools, and detect and fix Windows (CRLF) line endings.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-linux-system-intro}

Part I asked you to run several "system" commands on trust. In
@sec-orientation you pasted a block into `~/.bash_profile` (Mac) that
put the GNU tools first on your `PATH`. In @sec-book-setup the pixi
installer added a line to `~/.bashrc`, bare `seqkit` said `command not
found` while `pixi run seqkit` worked, and `export EDITOR=nano` lasted
only until the terminal closed. In @sec-organizing-projects,
`chmod a-w` made the raw reads read-only, yet `rm -f` could still delete
a read-only file in a writable folder. This chapter explains each of
these, so that when one goes wrong you know where to look.

The chapter has two halves, and it works well as two sittings. The
first is about **who may do what and how commands are found**:
permissions, making a script run, `PATH`, environment variables, and
the startup files that set them. The second is about **the running
system**: processes, disk space, the differences between Linux and
macOS tools, and Windows line endings.

Commands run on your laptop. Everything that changes files happens in a
scratch folder, `~/bioinf-computing-ch07`; in the project,
`~/bioinf-computing`, you only look (`ls -l`, `du`). Two things you will
deliberately change outside scratch: a few lines in your `~/.bashrc`
(@sec-linux-system-startup, with a backup first) and your notes in
`NOTEBOOK.md`. Make the scratch folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07 && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
```

Two sections and the first exercise also read the practice folder
`~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/` from @sec-shell-basics, without
changing it. If you do not have it, paste the setup block from
@sec-shell-basics-intro first.

The Linux outputs shown were captured on Ubuntu 24.04 (bash 5.2.21, GNU
coreutils 9.4, grep 3.11, sed 4.9, file 5.45), on a machine named
`laptop` with the user `you`; macOS outputs on macOS 15 with the Mac's
own tools, where the text says so. Ubuntu 26.04, which WSL installs in
late 2026, replaces most GNU core tools with a rewrite called uutils
(@sec-linux-system-gnu-bsd); where its output differs, the text says so.
Process numbers, dates, and sizes on your machine will differ.

## Who may do what: permissions {#sec-linux-system-permissions}

Every file and folder belongs to one **user** (its owner) and one
**group**, and carries three sets of permissions. Start with who you
are, then look at the raw reads you protected in
@sec-organizing-projects:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
whoami
id
cd ~/bioinf-computing
ls -ld data/raw
ls -l data/raw
```

```{.console}
you
uid=1000(you) gid=1000(you) groups=1000(you)
dr-xr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 11:22 data/raw
total 4372
-r--r--r-- 1 you you     112 Nov 17 11:22 checksums.md5
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

`id` gives your user, your main group, and every group you belong to
(on your own laptop it may list more, such as `sudo`; on a cluster,
your lab's project groups). In `ls -l`, the two `you` columns are the
owner and the group (@fig-ls-long in @sec-shell-basics named them). The
first column is what this section explains.

**Now name the parts** (@fig-permission-string). After the type letter
(`d` folder, `-` file, `l` link) come three groups of three letters:
for the **user** who owns it, for members of its **group**, and for
**other** users. In each group, `r` is read, `w` is write, `x` is
execute, and `-` means "not allowed".

::: {#fig-permission-string}
{{< svg ../figures/permission-string.svg >}}

Two permission strings taken apart: the type letter, then the
user, group, and other triplets. Each triplet is also one digit, the
sum of 4 (`r`), 2 (`w`), and 1 (`x`). On a folder the same letters mean
something different (below).
:::

On a file the letters mean what you would guess: read its contents,
change its contents, run it as a program. On a **folder** they mean
something else, and that is where most surprises come from. Try it in
scratch, on a folder `d` holding one readable file, with the owner's
`x` removed:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm
mkdir d && echo hello > d/f
chmod u-x d # <1>
ls -ld d
\ls d # <2>
\ls -l d
cat d/f
cd d
chmod u+x d # <3>
```
1. `chmod` changes permissions: `u-x` removes (`-`) execute (`x`) for
   the user (`u`). The full syntax follows below.
2. The backslash runs `ls` without any alias your system defines
   (@sec-linux-system-path); a colouring alias can change what `ls`
   tries to read.
3. Put `x` back, so the folder works again.

```{.console}
drw-r-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 14:02 d
f
ls: cannot access 'd/f': Permission denied
total 0
-????????? ? ? ? ?            ? f
cat: d/f: Permission denied
bash: cd: d: Permission denied
```

(Ubuntu 26.04's `ls` shows the `?` line without the `cannot access`
message.) `ls d` still lists the name `f`: reading a folder means reading its
list of names, and you kept `r`. Everything *about* the entry fails:
`ls -l` cannot read its details (the question marks), `cat` cannot open
it although the file itself is readable, and `cd` cannot go in. On a
folder, `x` (often called **search** permission) is what lets you reach
the entries and pass through to anything below. The reverse also holds:
with `x` but no `r`, `ls d` says `cannot open directory 'd'`, yet `cat
d/f` works if you know the name. @tbl-permission-meaning collects the
cases.

: What each letter allows, on a file and on a folder, and the message
you get without it. {#tbl-permission-meaning}

| Letter | On a file | On a folder | Without it |
|:-------|:----------|:------------|:-----------|
| `r` | read the contents | list the names | `cat: f: Permission denied`; `ls: cannot open directory 'd'` |
| `w` | change the contents | add, remove, or rename entries (needs `x` too) | `bash: f: Permission denied` on `>`; `rm: cannot remove 'd/f'` |
| `x` | run it as a program | reach the entries, `cd` into it, pass through | `bash: ./f: Permission denied`; `cd: d: Permission denied` |

Two rules make the letters predictable:

- **The classes are chosen, not added up.** If you own the file, only
  the user triplet counts. An owner without `x` is refused even when
  "other" has `x`.
- **You need `x` on every folder on the way.** `cat
  ~/a/b/c/file.txt` needs `x` on `a`, `b`, and `c` as well as `r` on the
  file.

**Deleting is a change to the folder.** Now @sec-organizing-projects's
surprise has its explanation. Removing a file takes its name out of the
folder's list, so `rm` needs `w` and `x` on the **folder**; the file's
own permissions do not matter. Creating a new file is also a change to
the folder. Changing an existing file is not:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir locked && echo old > locked/data.txt
chmod a-w locked
echo new > locked/data.txt; cat locked/data.txt
echo x > locked/new.txt
rm locked/data.txt
chmod u+w locked
```

```{.console}
new
bash: locked/new.txt: Permission denied
rm: cannot remove 'locked/data.txt': Permission denied
```

The folder is read-only, yet `data.txt` was overwritten, because the
file itself was still writable: only a new name or a removed name
changes the folder. That is why @sec-organizing-projects protected the
files **and** the folder with `chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw`. It also
explains @sec-text-tools's redirect into `data/raw/`: `echo test >
data/raw/notes.txt` makes a new name, which the folder refuses; `sort …
> data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` targets an existing file, which the
file's missing `w` refuses.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
On a folder, `r` lists the names, `x` lets you reach the entries, and
`w` (with `x`) lets you add, remove, or rename them. A file's own
permissions do not protect it from deletion; its folder's do.
:::

These are the ordinary permissions on your own disk. On a cluster, two
more things can explain a refusal the letters do not: access control
lists (ACLs), which grant extra users or groups access, and storage
mounted so that nothing on it may run as a program, which turns
`./script.sh` into `Permission denied` whatever its letters say. If the
string looks right and you are still refused, ask the help desk
(@sec-getting-help).

### Changing permissions with `chmod`

`chmod` takes a change and one or more names. The **symbolic** form
says who, how, and what:

- who: `u` (user), `g` (group), `o` (other), `a` (all three);
- how: `+` add, `-` remove, `=` set exactly;
- what: `r`, `w`, `x`.

You have used it twice already: `chmod a-w` (remove write for all,
@sec-organizing-projects) and `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` (@sec-book-setup). The
second is the **octal** form: one digit per class, each the sum of
`r` = 4, `w` = 2, `x` = 1 (@fig-permission-string). So `7` = `rwx`,
`6` = `rw-`, `5` = `r-x`, `4` = `r--`, `0` = `---`, and `700` means the
owner may do everything and nobody else anything. GNU `stat` prints
both forms:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
touch notes.txt && mkdir private
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt private # <1>
chmod u+x notes.txt && ls -l notes.txt
chmod 644 notes.txt && ls -l notes.txt
chmod go-rx private && stat -c '%A %a %n' private
umask
```
1. `-c` gives a format: `%A` the string, `%a` the octal number, `%n`
   the name. (macOS's own `stat` has different options:
   @sec-linux-system-gnu-bsd.)

```{.console}
-rw-r--r-- 644 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x 755 private
-rwxr--r-- 1 you you 0 Nov 17 14:04 notes.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 0 Nov 17 14:04 notes.txt
drwx------ 700 private
0022
```

A symbolic change **modifies** the current permissions (`u+x` added one
letter to whatever was there); an octal number **sets** all nine at
once. So the same `chmod a-w` gave `555` on @sec-organizing-projects's
folder and `444` on its files only because they started at `755` and
`644`. Why do new files start at `644` and folders at `755`? Your
**umask**, `0022`, removes `w` for group and other from every new file
and folder. Sites can set a different umask: Nova's is `0002`, which
leaves `w` for the group, so new files start at `664` and folders at
`775`, and your lab can edit them. SCINet's Ceres sets `0027`, so new
files start at `640` and folders at `750`: your group can read them
but not change them, and other users cannot see them. On a cluster
that does this, a labmate who must edit your file in a shared project
folder needs you to run `chmod g+w` on it (@tbl-chmod-recipes). Check
yours with `umask`; you rarely need to change it.

: Common permission changes. The "before" column matters for symbolic
changes, which modify the current mode. {#tbl-chmod-recipes}

| Goal | Before | Command | After |
|:-----|:-------|:--------|:------|
| Protect raw data | `-rw-r--r--` (644), folder `drwxr-xr-x` (755) | `chmod a-w files folder` | `-r--r--r--` (444), `dr-xr-xr-x` (555) |
| Make a script runnable by you | `-rw-r--r--` (644) | `chmod u+x script.sh` | `-rwxr--r--` (744) |
| Private folder (`~/.ssh`) | any | `chmod 700 folder` | `drwx------` |
| Private key file | any | `chmod 600 file` | `-rw-------` |
| Let your group read a tree | `-rw-------`, `drwx------` | `chmod -R g+rX folder` | `-rw-r-----`, `drwxr-x---` |
| Undo a change | (note it first) | `stat -c '%a' name`, then `chmod <that number> name` | as before |

There is no general "undo" for `chmod`: note the old mode first if you
might want it back. Two more details for whole trees:

- `-R` applies a change to a folder and everything inside it. `chmod -R
  a+x folder` makes every data file "executable" too (try it on a
  scratch folder and `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-xr-x` on plain files).
- A capital `X` adds `x` only to folders and to files that are already
  executable for someone, and leaves ordinary data files alone. That is
  why `g+rX` in the table is safe on a tree of data.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `chmod -R 777` is not a fix
`777` lets every user on the machine change or delete your files. When
you get `Permission denied`, read the permission string, find which
letter is missing for whom, and add only that.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "When I get `Permission denied`, `chmod 777` or `sudo` fixes it"
**Reality.** It hides which permission was missing and removes the
protection for everyone. On a cluster you cannot use `sudo` at all.
Read the string, then change one letter.
:::

### Try it: three ways to write the same permissions

@fig-permission-calculator shows the string, the octal number, and the
symbolic `chmod` for any combination. Tick boxes and watch all three
change; switch between file and folder to see what the letters mean.
Try making `750`, then `644`, then the folder setting `700`.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof permKind = Inputs.radio(["file", "folder"], {label: "Permissions on a", value: "file"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof permUser = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "user (owner)", value: ["r", "w"]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof permGroup = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "group", value: ["r"]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof permOther = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "other", value: ["r"]})
```

::: {#fig-permission-calculator}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const classes = [
    {name: "user", key: "u", bits: permUser},
    {name: "group", key: "g", bits: permGroup},
    {name: "other", key: "o", bits: permOther}
  ];
  const letters = ["r", "w", "x"];
  const value = {r: 4, w: 2, x: 1};
  const isDir = permKind === "folder";
  const str = (isDir ? "d" : "-") + classes.map((c) =>
    letters.map((l) => c.bits.includes(l) ? l : "-").join("")).join("");
  const octal = classes.map((c) =>
    c.bits.reduce((s, l) => s + value[l], 0)).join("");
  const sym = classes.map((c) =>
    c.key + "=" + letters.filter((l) => c.bits.includes(l)).join("")).join(",");
  const name = isDir ? "folder" : "file.txt";
  const fileWords = {r: "read it", w: "change it", x: "run it"};
  const dirWords = {r: "list names", w: "add/remove entries", x: "reach entries"};
  const say = (c) => {
    const w = isDir ? dirWords : fileWords;
    const can = letters.filter((l) => c.bits.includes(l)).map((l) => w[l]);
    if (isDir && c.bits.includes("w") && !c.bits.includes("x"))
      return can.join(", ") + " (but w is useless without x)";
    return can.length ? can.join(", ") : "nothing";
  };
  const box = 40, gap = 6, groupGap = 30, left = 60, top = 40;
  const gx = (i) => left + i * (3 * box + 2 * gap + groupGap);
  return htl.svg`<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 720 300" role="img"
      aria-label="${`${str}, octal ${octal}, chmod ${sym}`}">
    <text x="${left - 40}" y="${top + 27}" font-size="22" class="mono fill-muted">${isDir ? "d" : "-"}</text>
    ${classes.map((c, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <text x="${gx(i) + (3 * box + 2 * gap) / 2}" y="${top - 12}" font-size="13"
            text-anchor="middle" class="fill-muted">${c.name}</text>
      ${letters.map((l, j) => {
        const on = c.bits.includes(l);
        return htl.svg`<g>
          <rect x="${gx(i) + j * (box + gap)}" y="${top}" width="${box}" height="${box}" rx="5"
                class="${on ? "fill-given-soft stroke-given" : "fill-surface stroke-line"}"/>
          <text x="${gx(i) + j * (box + gap) + box / 2}" y="${top + 27}" font-size="20"
                text-anchor="middle" class="mono ${on ? "fill-given" : "fill-muted"}">${on ? l : "-"}</text>
        </g>`;})}
      <text x="${gx(i) + (3 * box + 2 * gap) / 2}" y="${top + box + 26}" font-size="18"
            text-anchor="middle" class="mono">${c.bits.reduce((s, l) => s + value[l], 0)}</text>
    </g>`)}
    <text x="20" y="${top + 120}" font-size="15">String: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">${str}</tspan></text>
    <text x="20" y="${top + 146}" font-size="15">Octal: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">chmod ${octal} ${name}</tspan></text>
    <text x="20" y="${top + 172}" font-size="15">Symbolic: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">chmod ${sym} ${name}</tspan></text>
    ${classes.map((c, i) => htl.svg`<text x="20" y="${top + 204 + i * 20}" font-size="13.5" class="fill-muted">${c.name}: ${say(c)}</text>`)}
  </svg>`;
}
```

A permission calculator. The nine boxes are the letters of the string;
each class's digit is the sum of 4 (`r`), 2 (`w`), and 1 (`x`). The
two `chmod` lines set exactly these permissions, in octal and in
symbolic form.
:::

If the figure does not load, the lesson is in @fig-permission-string:
`rwxr-x---`, `750`, and `u=rwx,g=rx,o=` say the same thing.

### Groups and shared folders

On a cluster, a lab shares files through a Unix **group**: a project
folder such as `/project/<name>` on SCINet or `/work/<group>` on Nova
belongs to the lab's group, and members get the group's permissions
(@sec-cluster-sites has each site's details). When a labmate cannot
read your file, check two things: which group owns it (`ls -l`) and
whether that group may read it (the middle triplet). `id` shows which
groups you are in; `chgrp <group> file` changes a file's group to one
of yours.

Two special settings appear on shared folders. You will mostly meet
them, not set them; the site usually does:

: Two special permissions on shared folders (overview). {#tbl-special-bits}

| Setting | Shown as | On a folder |
|:--------|:---------|:------------|
| set-group-ID (setgid), `chmod g+s` | `s` in the group's `x` place: `drwxrws---` | new files and folders inside get the folder's group instead of your main group |
| sticky, `chmod +t` | `t` in other's `x` place: `drwxrwxrwt` (as on `/tmp`) | in a folder everyone may write, only an entry's owner may delete or rename it |

Setgid decides the group of a new file, not whether the group may read
it: the new file's permissions still come from your umask (and any
default ACLs). If files you create in a project folder come out
unreadable to your lab, check their group and permissions with `ls -l`
and ask the help desk what the site expects.

Here is what this looks like on Nova, in a group folder and a lab folder
inside it (names replaced by `<group>`, `<lab>`, and `you`):

```bash
ls -ld /work/<group> /work/<group>/<lab>
cd /work/<group>/<lab>
touch group_test && ls -l group_test
umask
```

```
drwxrws--T. 43 root its-hpc-nova-<group> 44 Nov 18 12:11 /work/<group>
drwxrwsr-x. 16 you  its-hpc-nova-<group> 16 Nov 16 18:24 /work/<group>/<lab>
-rw-rw-r--. 1 you its-hpc-nova-<group> 0 Nov 20 12:34 group_test
0002
```

Both folders have the setgid `s`, so the new file belongs to the lab's
group, not to your main group (`domain users` on Nova). It is `rw-rw-r--`
because Nova's umask is `0002`, so your labmates can edit it. The group
folder also has a capital `T`. That is the sticky bit on a folder that
others can't enter (no `x` for other); a lowercase `t` means the sticky
bit plus `x`. The `.` after each permission string means the file has
an SELinux security label, which you can ignore. Delete the test file
with `rm group_test` when you are done.

SCINet's Ceres follows the same pattern in `/project/<name>`, owned by
`root` and the group `proj-<name>`, with two differences. Your main
group there is a personal group named after you, so without the setgid
`s` your files would belong to a group nobody else is in. And the
umask is `0027`, so the same `touch` gives `-rw-r-----`, and a folder
you make gives `drwxr-s---`: your lab can read and enter, but not edit
or add files, until you run `chmod g+w` on them.

The [GNU coreutils
manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/File-permissions.html)
describes all of this in full.

**Administrators and `sudo`.** On your laptop, `sudo` runs one command
as the administrator (`root`), for changes to the system itself, such
as installing packages with `apt`. Never use it to fix permissions on
your own files: files created by `root` in your home folder are a new
problem. On a cluster you are not an administrator and this book never
needs `sudo`: the book environment and later ones install into your own
folders (@sec-book-setup, @sec-environments).

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** (a) A folder is `drwxr-xr-x` and owned by you; a
file in it is `-r--r--r--`. Can you delete the file? (b) What does
`chmod 640 notes.txt` give, as a string? (c) A folder you own is
`drw-r--r--`. Can you `cat` a readable file inside it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
(a) Yes. Deleting changes the folder, where you have `w` and `x`; the
file's own permissions do not matter. `rm` asks first because the file
is read-only; `rm -f` does not ask. (b) `-rw-r-----`: you read and
write, the group reads, others get nothing. (c) No. Without `x` on the
folder you can list the names but not reach the entries.
:::
:::

## Making a script run {#sec-linux-system-scripts}

@sec-organizing-projects ran its script as `pixi run bash
src/01_count_reads.sh`: `bash` read the file. Scripts can also run as
commands of their own. Make a one-line script in scratch (with nano or
VS Code, or paste this) and try four ways to run it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf 'echo "hello from $0"\n' > hello.sh # <1>
bash hello.sh
./hello.sh
chmod u+x hello.sh
./hello.sh
hello.sh
```
1. `$0` is the name the script was started as (@sec-shell-scripts).

```{.console}
hello from hello.sh
bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied
hello from ./hello.sh
bash: hello.sh: command not found
```

: Four ways to run the same file. {#tbl-run-attempts}

| Command | Result | Exit status | Why |
|:--------|:-------|:-----------:|:----|
| `bash hello.sh` | runs | 0 | `bash` reads the file; it need not be executable |
| `./hello.sh` | `Permission denied` | 126 | found, but not allowed to run: no `x` |
| `chmod u+x hello.sh`, then `./hello.sh` | runs | 0 | now executable |
| `hello.sh` | `command not found` | 127 | without a `/`, bash searches `PATH`, and this folder is not on it (@sec-linux-system-path) |

The exit statuses join @sec-getting-help's `echo $?`: **126** means
"found but cannot run", **127** "not found". `./hello.sh` works because
`.` is the current folder, so `./hello.sh` is a path, and a name with a
`/` in it is run directly, with no search.

**The shebang line.** Add one line at the very top of the file:

```{.bash filename="hello.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "hello from $0"
```

When a file with the `x` bit is run, the kernel reads its first line.
If it starts with `#!` (said "shebang"), the rest names the program that
should read the file, and the kernel starts that program with the
file's name (@fig-run-a-script). Without a shebang, bash happens to run
the file as a bash script, but other programs that start it may not;
always write one. It must be the very first line, starting at the first
character.

::: {#fig-run-a-script}
{{< svg ../figures/run-a-script.svg >}}

What happens when you type `./hello.sh`. A path skips the `PATH`
search; the kernel checks the `x` bit, reads the shebang line, and
`env` finds `bash`. The last step shows a file saved with Windows line
endings, whose shebang names a program that does not exist
(@sec-linux-system-line-endings). Use *Next* to step through.
:::

This book's scripts use `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, as @sec-organizing-projects's
script already does. `env` looks `bash` up on your `PATH`, so on a Mac
it finds the current bash from @sec-orientation instead of Apple's
`/bin/bash`, which is version 3.2 from 2007 (`/bin/bash --version` on a
Mac prints `GNU bash, version 3.2.57`). Inside `pixi run` or `pixi
shell` it finds the environment's programs the same way. R and Python
scripts follow the same pattern, `#!/usr/bin/env Rscript` and
`#!/usr/bin/env python3` (@sec-r-essentials, @sec-python-essentials).

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "To run a script I must type `bash script.sh`"
**Reality.** With a shebang line and the `x` bit, a script runs as
`./script.sh`, and by name alone once its folder is on `PATH`.
`bash script.sh` ignores the shebang: `bash plot.py` tries to read
Python as shell commands and fails.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A command runs as a program when the shell can find it (a path, or a
folder on `PATH`), the file has the `x` bit, and its first line names
an interpreter that exists.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `./run.sh` says `Permission denied`, but `bash
run.sh` works. What is missing, and what is the fix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The `x` bit. `bash run.sh` only needs to read the file; `./run.sh`
needs permission to run it. `chmod u+x run.sh`.
:::
:::

## How the shell finds a command: `PATH` {#sec-linux-system-path}

When you type a name without a `/`, such as `ls` or `seqkit`, bash looks
for a program file with that name in a list of folders. The list is the
variable `PATH`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' # <1>
```
1. `PATH` is one line with folders separated by `:`; `tr` turns each
   `:` into a newline (@sec-text-tools).

```{.console}
/home/you/.pixi/bin
/usr/local/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/sbin
/usr/bin
/sbin
/bin
```

Bash searches these folders **in order, top to bottom, and runs the
first match**. `~/.pixi/bin` is first because @sec-book-setup's pixi
installer added it to the front. Your list will be longer or ordered
differently: Ubuntu adds `/usr/games` and `/snap/bin`, and on a Mac
after @sec-orientation the GNU folders come first.

**Which copy runs?** `type -a` asks bash for every match, in the order
bash would use them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
type -a ls
type cd
```

```{.console}
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
ls is /usr/bin/ls
ls is /bin/ls
cd is a shell builtin
```

Three kinds of answer appear here. An **alias** is a shortcut bash
expands before anything else: on Ubuntu, and on Nova, typing `ls`
really runs `ls --color=auto`, which colours the names. Then come the
program files on `PATH`: two here, because current Ubuntu keeps `/bin`
as another name for `/usr/bin`, so both entries reach the same file.
And `cd` is a **builtin**, part of bash, with no file at all
(@sec-shell-basics). On a Mac after @sec-orientation the answer
differs:

```{.console}
ls is /usr/local/opt/coreutils/libexec/gnubin/ls
ls is /bin/ls
```

The GNU `ls` comes first, then Apple's own (`/opt/homebrew/…` on Apple
silicon). That order is what @sec-orientation's `gnubin` lines
arranged.

So the full order is: aliases, then functions (named groups of commands,
@sec-shell-scripts), then builtins, then the folders of `PATH`.
Changing `PATH` cannot override an alias or builtin of the same name.
`alias` alone lists your aliases; a backslash (`\ls`) or `command ls`
runs the program without the alias, as you did in
@sec-linux-system-permissions.

**The book's environment.** Now the explanation @sec-book-setup
promised. From the project folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
type -a seqkit
pixi run bash -c 'type -a seqkit; echo "$PATH" | tr ":" "\n" | head -n 3'
```

```{.console}
bash: type: seqkit: not found
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
/home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin
/home/you/.pixi/bin
/usr/local/sbin
```

No folder on your `PATH` holds `seqkit`, hence @sec-getting-help's
`command not found`. `pixi run` starts one command with the
environment's `bin` folder put **first** on `PATH`, so the
environment's copy is found and wins over any other. `pixi shell` does
the same for a whole new shell, until you type `exit`
(@fig-path-search).

::: {#fig-path-search}
{{< svg ../figures/path-search.svg >}}

How bash finds `seqkit`: it checks each `PATH` folder from the top and
runs the first match. In a plain terminal nothing matches; `pixi run`
puts the environment's folder on top; a second copy higher up would
win instead; `type -a` lists every match in order. Use *Next* to step
through.
:::

**The wrong copy.** If two copies are on `PATH`, the first wins, even
if it is older. This is what @sec-getting-help warned about: a bare
`seqkit` might run some other installation, with a different version.
Check with `type -a seqkit` and `seqkit version`; inside the book,
`pixi run` makes the environment's copy win. On a cluster, `module
load` also works by changing `PATH` (@sec-hpc-slurm), so a module
loaded beside `pixi shell` can put a second copy in front.
Exercise 3 sets up a fake `seqkit` to show this safely.

`which seqkit` is a common alternative, but it is a separate program,
its versions behave differently, and its answer need not match what
bash will run. Usually it knows nothing of your aliases; on Nova
`which ls` shows the alias too, because there `type which` reports
`which is a function`: the site wraps the real `/usr/bin/which` in a
shell function that passes it your aliases and functions. Use bash's
own `type -a`. @tbl-finding-commands collects the commands.

: Commands for finding out what runs. {#tbl-finding-commands}

| Command | Tells you | Use it when |
|:--------|:----------|:------------|
| `type -a name` | every alias, builtin, and file bash would use, in order | first choice, in bash |
| `type name` | the one bash will use | a quick check |
| `command -v name` | what will run, in one line | in scripts (@sec-shell-scripts) |
| `which name` | a file on `PATH`, by a separate program | other people's notes; prefer `type -a` |
| `echo "$PATH" \| tr ':' '\n'` | the folders searched, in order | `command not found` |
| `hash -r` | (forgets remembered locations) | after moving or installing a program in the same terminal |

The last row: bash remembers where it found each command, so after you
move or install a program, `hash -r` (or a new terminal) makes it look
again.

**Changing `PATH`.** Put a folder of your own **in front** of the
existing list:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
```

`$PATH` on the right is the old list, so this adds one folder and keeps
the rest. It is the same shape as the `gnubin` line in
@sec-orientation's `~/.bash_profile` and the line the pixi installer
added to `~/.bashrc`. It lasts for this terminal only;
@sec-linux-system-startup makes such lines permanent. Two mistakes to
avoid:

- **Replacing instead of adding.** `PATH=~/bin` leaves only one folder,
  and every ordinary command fails with `command not found`. Open a new
  terminal to recover, or run `export PATH=/usr/bin:/bin` to get the
  basics back.
- **Putting `.` (the current folder) on `PATH`.** Then whatever folder
  you are in can supply a program called `ls`. Type `./script.sh`
  instead.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
For a name without a `/`, bash checks aliases, functions, and builtins,
then searches the `PATH` folders top to bottom and runs the first match.
`type -a` shows every match in that order.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "Once I install a tool, it works in every terminal"
**Reality.** (From @sec-book-setup, now with the mechanism.) A tool
runs by name only if its folder is on that shell's `PATH`. The book
environment's folder is added by `pixi run` and `pixi shell`, for that
command or shell only; a module's by `module load`.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `type -a samtools` prints `samtools is
/home/you/bin/samtools`, then `samtools is /usr/bin/samtools`. Which runs
when you type `samtools`, and how would you run the other one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The first, `~/bin/samtools`, because `~/bin` comes earlier on `PATH`.
Run the other by its path, `/usr/bin/samtools`.
:::
:::

## Environment variables {#sec-linux-system-variables}

`PATH` is one of many **variables** the shell keeps. Look at a few:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "$HOME"
echo "$USER"
echo "$SHELL"
```

```{.console}
/home/you
you
/bin/bash
```

`env | sort | less` lists the dozens of variables that every program
started from this shell receives, one `NAME=value` per line (`q`
quits). Now see the difference between a variable that stays in the
shell and one that is passed on. `bash -c '…'` starts a second bash, a
**child** of this one, that runs one line and exits:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
x=1
bash -c 'echo "child sees x=[$x]"'
export x
bash -c 'echo "child sees x=[$x]"'
```

```{.console}
child sees x=[]
child sees x=[1]
```

**Now name it.** `x=1` makes a **shell variable**, which lives only in
this shell. `export` turns it into an **environment variable**, which
is copied into every program this shell starts: scripts, R, Python,
seqkit. Copies only go down, from parent to child. A script cannot
change the variables of the shell that started it, which is why `pixi
shell` has to start a new shell rather than change yours. A second
terminal opened separately is not a child of the first, so it never
sees an `export` you typed in the first. Once a variable is exported
it stays exported: a later `x=2` changes the value children see,
without a second `export`. That is why `PATH`, already exported when
your shell starts, can be changed with a plain assignment.

Two details. No spaces around `=`: `x = 1` runs a command called `x`
(`bash: x: command not found`); quoting and the rest are
@sec-shell-scripts. And `SHELL` names your configured login shell, not
necessarily the shell you are typing in; to check you are in bash, use
@sec-orientation's `echo "$BASH_VERSION"`.

A variable can last for one command, one terminal, or every new
terminal (@tbl-variable-lifetime).

: How long a variable lasts. {#tbl-variable-lifetime}

| Set with | Lasts for | Seen by programs it starts? | Example |
|:---------|:----------|:---------------------------:|:--------|
| `NAME=value command` | that one command | yes, that command | `LC_ALL=C sort file` (@sec-text-tools) |
| `NAME=value` | this shell | no, unless already exported | `x=1` |
| `export NAME=value` | this shell | yes | `export EDITOR=nano` (@sec-book-setup) |
| a line in `~/.bashrc` | every new interactive shell | if exported | @sec-linux-system-startup |

::: {.callout-tip}
## A setting for one command
Write the variable in front of the command, with no `export`:
`TMPDIR=~/bigtmp sort big.txt` gives `sort` a different folder for its
temporary files, for that run only.
:::

@tbl-common-variables lists the variables you will meet in this book.

: Environment variables you will meet. {#tbl-common-variables}

| Variable | Holds | Used by | More in |
|:---------|:------|:--------|:--------|
| `HOME` | your home folder; `~` means this | everything | @sec-shell-basics |
| `USER` | your user name | scripts, `ps -u "$USER"` | @sec-linux-system-processes |
| `PATH` | folders searched for commands | the shell | this chapter |
| `PWD` | the current folder | the shell, `pwd` | @sec-shell-basics |
| `SHELL` | your login shell | terminal programs | this section |
| `EDITOR` | the editor tools open for you | git, crontab | @sec-book-setup, @sec-git |
| `TMPDIR` | where temporary files go | `sort`, `samtools sort`, many tools | @sec-sam-bam-cram, @sec-hpc-slurm |
| `LANG`, `LC_ALL` | language, sort order, number format | `sort`, messages | below; @sec-numbers-encodings |
| `PIXI_CACHE_DIR` | where pixi keeps downloaded packages | pixi | @sec-book-setup |
| `SLURM_*` | job details inside a cluster job | your job scripts | @sec-hpc-slurm |

**Your locale settings.** @sec-text-tools used `LC_ALL=C sort` to get
the same sort order everywhere. The **locale** is the group of
`LANG` and `LC_*` variables that sets language, sort order, and number
format; `locale` prints yours:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
locale | head -n 6
```

```{.console}
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
LANGUAGE=
LC_CTYPE="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_NUMERIC="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_TIME="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_COLLATE="en_US.UTF-8"
```

`LC_COLLATE` is the one that decides sort order; `LC_ALL`, if set,
overrides all the others. This book leaves your default alone and sets
`LC_ALL=C` in front of a single command when the order must be
reproducible. A cluster may use a different default (often `C` or
`en_US.UTF-8`), so check `locale` there too. Text encodings themselves
are @sec-numbers-encodings.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `export THREADS=4` in one terminal, then
open a second terminal and run `echo "$THREADS"`. What prints, and
what would make the setting reach every new terminal?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
An empty line. `export` reaches the shell it was typed in and the
programs that shell starts; a separately opened terminal is not one of
them. A line `export THREADS=4` in `~/.bashrc` reaches every new
terminal.
:::
:::

## Startup files: `.bashrc` and `.bash_profile` {#sec-linux-system-startup}

Every time bash starts, it may first read a **startup file** of
commands from your home folder. That is how the pixi installer's
`PATH` line reaches every new terminal. Which file it reads depends on
two questions about how bash was started. Ask them in the terminal you
have open, and in a second bash started inside it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
shopt -q login_shell && echo login || echo "not login"
[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interactive || echo "not interactive"
bash -l -c 'shopt -q login_shell && echo login || echo "not login"'
bash -c '[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interactive || echo "not interactive"'
```

```{.console}
not login
interactive
login
not interactive
```

(Copy these as they are; `&&` and `||` are @sec-shell-scripts.) This
output is from a terminal window on desktop Ubuntu, which is
**interactive** (you type into it) but **not a login** shell; so is VS
Code's terminal on Linux and WSL, and a `bash` typed inside a shell.
`bash -l` starts a login shell, and a `bash -c` that just runs a line
is not interactive. An SSH login is both login and interactive; so is
a new Ubuntu window on WSL (Windows Terminal, or `wsl` typed in
PowerShell), a new Terminal window on a Mac, and VS Code's terminal on
a Mac with @sec-book-setup's `-l` setting. There the first line says
`login`, and bash's own messages start with `-bash:` instead of
`bash:`. Run
the first two lines in each place you open a shell, including your
cluster, to see what yours are.

**Now name it** (@tbl-startup-files, @fig-startup-files). These are the
rules from the [Bash
manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bash-Startup-Files.html)
for the cases you will meet:

: Which of your startup files bash reads. {#tbl-startup-files}

| How bash starts | Example | Reads |
|:----------------|:--------|:------|
| interactive login | SSH login; new WSL window; Mac Terminal; `bash -l` | the **first one that exists** of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile` |
| interactive, not login | new desktop Ubuntu terminal; VS Code's terminal on Linux/WSL; `bash` typed in a shell | `~/.bashrc` |
| not interactive (a script) | `bash script.sh`, `./script.sh`, a job script | neither (unless the variable `BASH_ENV` names a file) |
| a command over SSH | `ssh host command` | often `~/.bashrc` (bash's special case for remote commands; Nova and Ceres do) |

::: {#fig-startup-files}
{{< svg ../figures/startup-files.svg >}}

Which startup file bash reads, by how it was started. A login shell
reads the first of three files that exists; an interactive non-login
shell reads `~/.bashrc`; a script reads neither. In the book's setup
the login file reads `~/.bashrc` too, so settings in `~/.bashrc` reach
every interactive shell.
:::

System-wide files such as `/etc/profile` are read as well; they are
set by whoever runs the machine (@sec-cluster-sites for the clusters).

**The book's setup.** Login and non-login shells read different files,
which would mean writing every setting twice. Instead, the login file
reads `~/.bashrc`:

- on a Mac, the last lines of @sec-orientation's `~/.bash_profile`
  block do it (`if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi`; `.` reads
  a file into the current shell);
- on Ubuntu and WSL, the `~/.profile` that comes with a new account
  does the same;
- on a cluster, the site's default files usually do; check (below).

So **put your settings in `~/.bashrc`**, and every interactive shell
gets them. Now reread @sec-orientation's block line by line: Homebrew's
`shellenv` sets `PATH` for Homebrew, the `gnubin` loop puts the GNU
tools first and the `export` passes `PATH` and `MANPATH` on, and the
last line reads `~/.bashrc`.

One trap on Ubuntu, WSL, and clusters: bash reads only the *first* login
file that exists. If you create a `~/.bash_profile` (even an empty one),
bash stops reading `~/.profile`, and with it the line that reads
`~/.bashrc`. Check which files you have:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls -a ~ | grep -E '^\.(bash|profile)' # <1>
grep -n bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile 2>/dev/null # <2>
```
1. `grep -E` with a regular expression (@sec-text-tools): names
   starting with `.bash` or `.profile`.
2. Which login file reads `~/.bashrc`, and on which line;
   `2>/dev/null` hides the messages for files you do not have.

A script that sees one of your variables usually **inherited** it from
the shell that started it (it was exported there); that does not mean
the script read `~/.bashrc`.

### Changing `~/.bashrc` safely

Make @sec-book-setup's `EDITOR` setting permanent. First a backup, with
`cp -n` so that a second try never overwrites the first backup
(@sec-shell-basics; ignore the `non-portable` warning Ubuntu's `cp`
prints):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07
echo 'export EDITOR=nano' >> ~/.bashrc # <1>
tail -n 2 ~/.bashrc
```
1. `>>` **appends**. A single `>` would replace your whole `~/.bashrc`
   with this one line (@sec-text-tools).

Then open a **new** terminal and check with `echo "$EDITOR"`. (To apply
the file to the terminal you are in, `source ~/.bashrc` reads it again;
a new terminal is the honest test.) Rules for every change:

- Back up first, and keep one working terminal open while you test in a
  new one. If a broken file stops new terminals from working, `bash
  --noprofile --norc` starts a clean shell to fix it from, or restore
  the backup.
- **Nothing in `~/.bashrc` should print text.** A command run over SSH
  may read it (@tbl-startup-files), and output there can break `rsync`
  and older `scp` (@sec-working-remotely). Put anything that prints
  inside `if [[ $- == *i* ]]; then … fi`, which runs only in
  interactive shells.
- **On a cluster, keep the site's lines,** and do not load modules or
  start environments from startup files: they would change every
  terminal and every remote command without asking, and make a job's
  software depend on your dotfiles (@sec-hpc-slurm, @sec-cluster-sites).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: a `.bashrc` that prints text
Output from `~/.bashrc` can break `rsync` and `scp`. Back up before
editing, keep a working terminal open, and test in a new one.
:::

**Things worth putting there.** A few settings earlier chapters
pointed here:

```{.bash filename="~/.bashrc (additions)"}
export EDITOR=nano                 # @sec-book-setup
HISTSIZE=10000                     # remember more history (@sec-shell-basics)
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth             # skip duplicates and lines starting with a space
alias ll='ls -l'                   # a shortcut of your own
PS1='\u@\h:\w\$ '                  # the prompt: user@host:folder$
```

- **History:** `HISTSIZE` is how many commands a shell remembers (Ubuntu
  sets 1000); `ignoreboth` skips repeated lines and lines you start
  with a space. These are the settings @sec-shell-basics mentioned.
- **Aliases:** `alias ll='ls -l'` makes `ll` mean `ls -l` (Ubuntu's
  default `~/.bashrc` already defines it as `ls -alF`). Aliases are
  used only in interactive shells, never in scripts, so do not rely on
  them in anything you share.
- **The prompt:** the prompt is the variable `PS1`. `\u` is your user,
  `\h` the machine, `\w` the folder, so the line above gives
  `you@laptop:~/bioinf-computing$`, the prompt @sec-shell-basics
  described. Try a new `PS1` in one terminal first; it disappears when
  you close it. Keep the host name in it on a cluster: it tells you
  whether you are on a login node or a compute node (@sec-hpc-slurm).
- **`noclobber`:** you could add `set -o noclobber` (@sec-text-tools),
  but this book does not, because later chapters overwrite files on
  purpose.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You added `export EDITOR=nano` to `~/.bashrc` on
the cluster, but a new SSH login does not see it. What do you check?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
An SSH login reads the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`,
`~/.profile` that exists. Find which one that is (`ls -a ~`), and
whether it reads `~/.bashrc` (`grep -n bashrc` on it). If not, add
`if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi` to that file.
:::
:::

## Processes {#sec-linux-system-processes}

Start a command that takes a while, and stop it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sleep 300 # <1>
```
1. `sleep` waits for the given number of seconds and does nothing
   else: a safe stand-in for a long analysis. Press {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}}
   while it waits.

```{.console}
^C
```

Then check its exit status with `echo $?`: **130**, the number a
command gets when {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} stops it. Now run it in the
**background** by ending the line with `&`, so the prompt comes back at
once, and look at what is running:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sleep 300 &
jobs
ps
kill %1
jobs
```

```{.console}
[1] 3219
[1]+  Running                 sleep 300 &
    PID TTY          TIME CMD
   3217 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
   3219 pts/0    00:00:00 sleep
   3220 pts/0    00:00:00 ps
[1]+  Terminated              sleep 300
```

`[1] 3219` is the **job number** (`1`, for this terminal) and the
**process ID** (PID, `3219`, for the whole machine). `jobs` lists this
terminal's jobs; `ps` lists the processes started from this terminal:
your shell, the `sleep`, and `ps` itself. `kill %1` ended job 1; `kill
3219` would have done the same by PID. (On a Mac, bash prints
`Terminated: 15`.)

**Now name it.** A **process** is a running program, with a PID, an
owner, and a parent: the process that started it, here your shell.
Every program you have run, from `ls` to `seqkit`, ran as a process
and ended. Your shell is a process too, and runs builtins such as `cd`
and `export` inside itself, without starting a new one
(@sec-shell-basics). @fig-process-states shows the states a process can
be in, and how you move it between them.

::: {#fig-process-states}
{{< svg ../figures/process-states.svg >}}

The life of a process started from your shell. `&` and `bg` run it in
the background, `fg` brings it back; {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} stops it, still
holding its memory, until `fg`, `bg`, or `kill`. {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} and
`kill` ask it to end; `kill -9` forces it.
:::

A program in the **foreground** has your keyboard; one in the
**background** runs while you type other commands. To stop a program,
the shell sends it a **signal** (@tbl-signals).

: Ways to stop a process, and what the program can do about each.
{#tbl-signals}

| Key or command | Signal | The program can | Use it |
|:---------------|:-------|:----------------|:-------|
| {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} | `SIGINT` (interrupt) | clean up first, or ignore it | to stop the foreground command |
| `kill PID` or `kill %1` | `SIGTERM` (terminate), the default | clean up first, or ignore it | to end a background or stuck process |
| `kill -9 PID` | `SIGKILL` | nothing: ended at once | last resort, when `kill` alone did not work |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} | `SIGTSTP` (stop) | (it pauses) | rarely on purpose; see the pitfall |

{{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} and `kill` **ask**: a well-written tool deletes its
half-written files and exits. `kill -9` cannot be caught, so the program
gets no chance to clean up: look for and delete partial output files
afterwards. You can signal only your own processes.

**Stopped is not ended.** {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} pauses the foreground
program and gives you the prompt back. It looks like a way out, but the
program is still there:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sleep 600
```

Press {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}}, then:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
jobs
ps -o pid,stat,rss,command # <1>
exit
```
1. `-o` chooses columns: `stat` the state (`T` stopped, `S` sleeping,
   `R` running), `rss` the memory it holds, in kB, `command` the
   command line. Linux also accepts `cmd`, but the Mac's `ps` does not.

```{.console}
^Z
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
    PID STAT   RSS COMMAND
   3217 S     4776 bash
   3221 T     1952 sleep 600
   3222 R+    4152 ps -o pid,stat,rss,command
exit
There are stopped jobs.
```

Bash refuses the first `exit` to warn you. (In a login shell, such as
a WSL window or a Mac Terminal, `exit` prints `logout` first.) Resume the job with `fg`
(foreground) or `bg` (background), or end it with `kill %1`. A large
analysis stopped with {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} keeps all its memory until
then.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} does not stop a program for good
It pauses it, still holding its memory. Use {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} to stop
a command; if you pressed {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}}, finish with `fg` or
`kill %1`.
:::

Some clusters switch {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} off (SCINet's Ceres leaves it
on). On Nova, a site startup
file (`/etc/profile.d/disable-control-z.sh`) runs `stty susp undef`,
so the key does nothing and the command keeps running: no paused jobs
are left holding memory on a shared login node. `stty -a` shows
`susp = <undef>` when the key is off, and `susp = ^Z` when it works.
Press {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} instead, which still works there.

**Watching the machine: `top`.** `top` shows the busiest processes,
updated every few seconds; `q` quits. Here two busy test processes run
alongside everything else (Linux `top`, sorted by CPU):

```{.console}
top - 14:25:42 up  9:05,  1 user,  load average: 0.38, 0.28, 0.19
Tasks:   9 total,   3 running,   5 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s):  6.7 us,  5.5 sy,  0.0 ni, 87.7 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
MiB Mem :   7837.4 total,   3956.1 free,   1369.3 used,   2810.8 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   1024.0 total,   1024.0 free,      0.0 used.   6468.1 avail Mem

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
   3233 you       20   0    5688   1820   1820 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.21 yes
   3232 you       20   0    5688   1836   1836 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.20 yes
```

The columns to read first:

- `%CPU`: in Linux `top`'s usual display, 100% is one logical CPU
  (@sec-orientation's cores and threads). A tool running on four
  threads can show about 400%.
- `RES`: the memory it really holds, in kB unless marked (`m`, `g`).
- `USER` and `COMMAND`: whose it is and what it is.

On Linux, press `M` to sort by memory and `P` by CPU. macOS `top` looks
different and sorts with `top -o cpu` or `top -o mem`
(@sec-linux-system-gnu-bsd). `htop`, where installed, is a friendlier
version with the same information; this book uses `top`, which every
system has.

**On a cluster.** Do not rely on a command started in an ordinary SSH
terminal surviving when the connection drops, and do not rely on
closing the window to stop everything you started either: what happens
depends on how the program was started and how it handles signals (the
[Bash manual's
*Signals*](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Signals.html)
has the rules). For work that must keep running, use the site's
persistent sessions (`tmux`, @sec-working-remotely), or submit it to the
scheduler as a job, whose life does not depend on your window at all
(@sec-hpc-slurm). On a login node, `ps -u "$USER"` or `top -u "$USER"`
lists only your own processes, so you can find and end leftovers. You
need the `-u`: on Nova, `top`'s header showed 41 users and 1,714
processes on one login node, and on Ceres 62 users and 1,165. (`top`
cuts long user names to eight characters, so `first.last` shows as
`first.+`; `-u` still takes the full name.)
Heavy work belongs in a job, not on the login node (@sec-orientation).

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "Closing the window decides whether my command keeps running"
**Reality.** Neither "it keeps going" nor "it always stops" is safe to
assume. Run long work in `tmux` (@sec-working-remotely) or as a
scheduler job (@sec-hpc-slurm), and check with `ps -u "$USER"`.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `top` shows your `python` at `400%` CPU. How many
CPUs is it using? And what is the difference between {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}}
and {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}}?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
About four logical CPUs, in Linux `top`'s usual display (100% is one).
{{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} asks the program to end; {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} only
pauses it, and it keeps its memory until `fg`, `bg`, or `kill`.
:::
:::

## Disk usage: `df` and `du` {#sec-linux-system-disk}

Two questions come up all the time: how much space is left, and what is
using it. @sec-orientation used `df -h ~` for the first:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
df -h ~
```

```{.console}
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdd       1007G  2.0G  954G   1% /
```

`df` reports a whole **filesystem**: one disk or storage area, named in
the first column and reached through the folder in the last. (Your
first column will differ: `/dev/nvme0n1p2` on a Linux laptop,
`/dev/disk3s1` on a Mac.) `df -h ~ /tmp` shows whether two folders sit
on the same filesystem. For the second question, `du` adds up what is
inside folders. Ask it about the project, including the hidden `.pixi`
folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
du -sh ~/bioinf-computing/* ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi | sort -h # <1>
```
1. `-s` one total per name, `-h` human units. `sort -h` is like
   @sec-text-tools's `sort -n`, but understands sizes such as `512K`
   and `1.2G` (with `-n`, `1.2G` would sort before `512K`).

```{.console}
4.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/NOTEBOOK.md
4.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml
4.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/README.md
8.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/logs
8.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/results
8.0K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/src
160K	/home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.lock
4.3M	/home/you/bioinf-computing/data
1.3G	/home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi
```

The book's software is three hundred times bigger than its data. Real
projects reverse that, but environments are never small, which is why
they belong on storage with room for them (@sec-book-setup).

**Now name it.** `df` answers "how full is this disk?"; `du` answers
"how much is in these folders?". Three details make `du` less obvious
than it looks:

- `ls -l` on a folder shows the size of its list of names (`4096`), not
  of its contents (@sec-shell-basics); `du` measures the contents.
- `du` reports space **used on disk**, rounded up to whole blocks, so a
  folder of small files uses more than the file sizes add up to:
  `du -sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1` says `12K` for files
  totalling 86 bytes (`du -sh --apparent-size` gives the sum of sizes).
- Files can share space. pixi keeps downloaded packages in a **cache**
  (`~/.cache/rattler` on Linux) and links the environment's files to
  it, so the same 1.3 GB shows up once: `du -sh ~/.cache/rattler
  ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi` counts it under whichever comes first (here
  `1.3G` for the cache, then `97M` for `.pixi`). `PIXI_CACHE_DIR`
  (@sec-book-setup) moves the cache; it does not move an environment
  that already exists.

@tbl-disk-commands gathers the questions.

: Disk questions and the commands that answer them. {#tbl-disk-commands}

| Question | Command | Read | On a cluster |
|:---------|:--------|:-----|:-------------|
| How full is the disk this folder is on? | `df -h folder` | `Avail`, `Use%` | often the whole shared system, not your share |
| What is big in here? | `du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h` | the last lines | run it on the folder you suspect, not on `/` |
| How big is one folder? | `du -sh folder` | the one total | slow on huge trees |
| What is my limit? | the site's quota command or usage file | used vs limit | @sec-hpc-slurm, @sec-cluster-sites |

(In the second row, `.[!.]*` matches hidden names such as `.pixi`
without matching `..`, @sec-shell-basics.)

**On a cluster** `df` on shared storage often shows the whole system,
many terabytes or petabytes, not your share. On Nova, `df -h ~` gives
`172.16.7.238:/stor014/home  14T  7.5T  5.9T  56% /home`: the home
folders of everyone, on another machine (the `address:/path` form
means network storage). Your real limit is a **quota** for your user
or project, which each site reports its own way (@sec-hpc-slurm,
@sec-cluster-sites). @tbl-cluster-quotas compares two clusters.

: Checking storage limits on two clusters (captured November 2026).
{#tbl-cluster-quotas}

| | Nova (ISU) | Ceres (SCINet) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Quota command | none (`quota -s` prints nothing) | `my_quotas`: home and every project you belong to, usage vs quota in GB |
| Home limit | 10 GB; check with `du -sh ~` | about 30 GB; `my_quotas` or `quota -s` |
| Group storage | `/work/<group>`; usage and quota in the file `/work/<group>/group_storage_usage`, updated hourly | `/project/<name>`; in `my_quotas` |
| `df -h` on group storage | shows the group's share | shows the project's quota as the size |

So `df` can mislead in both directions: on one folder it shows the
disk everyone shares, on another just your group's allowance. Trust the
site's own command or file ([ISU file
storage](https://research.it.iastate.edu/file-storage), [SCINet
project management](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/data/project-management)).

Quotas can also count files, not just bytes; `df -i` shows a whole filesystem's file slots (inodes), which is likewise
not your file-count quota. And `du` on a huge tree is slow and loads
storage that everyone shares, so point it at the folder you suspect.
`ncdu`, where installed, lets you browse sizes interactively.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Find what fills a folder
`du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5` lists the five largest items in
the current folder, hidden ones included. (If there are no hidden names, `du` says it
cannot access `.[!.]*`: the pattern matched nothing and was passed on
as it is, @sec-shell-basics.)
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `df -h` on a shared folder says `2.1P` available, but your
job fails with `Disk quota exceeded`. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
There `df` describes the whole shared filesystem. Your group's quota is a
separate, much smaller limit; check it the way your site says, with a
quota command or a usage file (@sec-cluster-sites). It may also be a limit on the number of files.
:::
:::

## GNU (Linux) and BSD (macOS) tools {#sec-linux-system-gnu-bsd}

@sec-orientation promised this section. Each command below works on
Linux and on a Mac after @sec-orientation's setup, but fails with a
Mac's **own** tools. Read each message and guess why before opening the
answer:

```{.console}
$ ls --version
ls: unrecognized option `--version'
usage: ls [-@ABCFGHILOPRSTUWXabcdefghiklmnopqrstuvwxy1%,] [--color=when] [-D format] [file ...]
$ cat -A samples.csv
cat: illegal option -- A
usage: cat [-belnstuv] [file ...]
$ stat -c '%a' samples.csv
stat: illegal option -- c
usage: stat [-FLnq] [-f format | -l | -r | -s | -x] [-t timefmt] [file ...]
$ sed -i 's/x/y/' samples.csv
sed: 1: "samples.csv": unterminated substitute pattern
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
These are the BSD versions of `ls`, `cat`, `stat`, and `sed` that come
with macOS (captured on macOS 15 with `/bin/bash` 3.2 and the system's
own tools). They do not know `--version`, `-A`, or `-c`. BSD `sed -i`
expects a suffix for a backup copy right after `-i`, so it took
`s/x/y/` as that suffix and the file name as the script: a confusing
message about something you did not mean. With GNU tools first on
`PATH`, the same commands work (`ls --version` prints `ls (GNU
coreutils) 9.11`).
:::

**Now name it.** The Linux systems you will use come with the **GNU**
versions of the core tools this book uses: `ls`, `cp`, `stat`, `sed`,
`grep`, `find`, `awk`, `sort`. (Not every Linux tool is GNU: `ps` and
`top` usually come from a package called procps.) macOS comes with
**BSD** versions: same names, mostly the same basic use, different
options and messages. @sec-orientation's `gnubin` lines put GNU first on
your Mac's `PATH`, so the book's commands work as written. To see which
you have, use `type -a` (@sec-linux-system-path) or `--version`: GNU
tools print a version, BSD tools usually reject the option.

**A third family on new Ubuntu.** From Ubuntu 25.10, and in 26.04 LTS
(what WSL installs in late 2026), `ls --version` prints `ls (uutils
coreutils) 0.8.0`. [uutils](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils) is a
rewrite of GNU's core tools in the Rust language that aims to accept
the same options; Ubuntu keeps GNU's `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, and `df`, and
`grep` and `sed` are still GNU ([release
notes](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/release-notes/26.04/summary-for-lts-users/)).
The book's commands work there; a few messages read differently, as
noted where they appear. Clusters still run GNU.

It still matters in three places:

- **Scripts from a colleague's Mac**, written for BSD tools (`sed -i ''`,
  `date -v`), fail on Linux, and the book's GNU commands fail on a Mac
  without the setup. The installed manual page (`man sed`) is the
  authority for what a Mac's own tool does.
- **`#!/bin/bash` on a Mac** means Apple's bash 3.2, which lacks
  features from 2009 on that @sec-shell-scripts may use. This book's
  `#!/usr/bin/env bash` avoids it.
- **Minimal containers** (@sec-containers) often have a third set,
  BusyBox, with fewer options still.

: Options you may meet that differ between GNU and BSD (overview).
{#tbl-gnu-bsd}

| Task | GNU (Linux) | BSD (macOS) | GNU form on a Mac's own tools |
|:-----|:------------|:------------|:-----------------|
| Edit a file in place | `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` | `sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f` | a confusing `sed: 1: …` error |
| Show invisible characters | `cat -A f` | `cat -et f` | `cat: illegal option -- A` |
| Permissions as a number | `stat -c '%a' f` | `stat -f '%Lp' f` | `stat: illegal option -- c` |
| A date from text | `date -d 2026-01-01` | `date -j -f %Y-%m-%d 2026-01-01` | `date: illegal option -- d` |
| Perl-style regular expressions | `grep -P` | (none) | `grep: invalid option -- P` |
| Sizes as file lengths | `du --apparent-size` | `du -A` | `du: unrecognized option` |

(Captured on macOS 15. Some older differences are gone: recent macOS
has `readlink -f`, `sort -h`, and `sort -V`.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## `--version` is a quick test
GNU tools answer `--version`; BSD tools usually refuse it. If a
command's options behave oddly on a Mac, check `type -a` first.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A colleague's script runs `sed -i 's/chr//'
genes.bed` and fails on a Mac without @sec-orientation's setup, with
`sed: 1: "genes.bed": …`. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The Mac's own `sed` is BSD `sed`, whose `-i` takes a backup suffix, so
it read `s/chr//` as the suffix and the file name as the script. Use GNU
`sed` (after the setup), or write `sed -i '' 's/chr//' genes.bed` for
BSD only.
:::
:::

## Line endings: LF and CRLF {#sec-linux-system-line-endings}

The practice folder from @sec-shell-basics has the same table twice:
`meta/samples.tsv` (tab-separated) and `meta/samples_from_excel.csv`
(comma-separated, as if saved from Excel). Ask both the same question:
how many rows have 30 reads?

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
grep -c $'\t30$' meta/samples.tsv # <1>
grep -c ',30$' meta/samples_from_excel.csv
```
1. `$'\t'` is bash's way to write a tab; `$` in the pattern is the end
   of the line (@sec-text-tools).

```{.console}
2
0
```

No error, and the CSV gives the wrong answer. `cat` shows nothing odd:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat meta/samples_from_excel.csv
cat -A meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3
cat -A meta/samples.tsv | head -n 3
```

```{.console}
sample,run_folder,condition,reads
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12
sample_A,run1,control,9
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_E,run5,treated,105
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_D,run4,control,8
sample,run_folder,condition,reads^M$
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12^M$
sample_A,run1,control,9^M$
sample^Irun_folder^Icondition^Ireads$
sample_C^IRun 3 final^Itreated^I12$
sample_A^Irun1^Icontrol^I9$
```

`cat -A` (@sec-text-tools used it to show tabs as `^I`) marks each line
end with `$`. In the CSV every line ends in `^M$`: an invisible
**carriage return** character (`\r`) before the newline. So the line
ends in `30\r`, not `30`, and `,30$` does not match (@fig-line-endings).

::: {#fig-line-endings}
{{< svg ../figures/line-endings.svg >}}

The same row in the two files. `cat` shows them alike; `cat -A` shows
the CSV's extra carriage return (`^M`), which sticks to the last field,
so a pattern anchored at the line end finds nothing.
:::

**The damage sticks to the last field.** Fields in the middle are clean;
the last one carries the `\r`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -d, -f2 meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3 | cat -A
f=$(sed -n 3p meta/samples_from_excel.csv | cut -d, -f4) # <1>
printf '%q\n' "$f" # <2>
[ "$f" = 9 ] && echo same || echo different
```
1. Store the `reads` field of line 3 in `f`. `$( )` and variables are
   @sec-shell-scripts; copy this as it is.
2. `%q` prints a value with invisible characters spelled out.

```{.console}
run_folder$
Run 3 final$
run1$
$'9\r'
different
```

The value is `9\r`, so a comparison with `9` is silently false. When
the last column holds file names, the result is a "missing" file that
is plainly there. A two-line sheet in scratch shows it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf 'sample,fastq_1\r\nWT_REP1,SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz\r\n' > sheet.csv
ls ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/$(tail -n 1 sheet.csv | cut -d, -f2)
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access '/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz'$'\r': No such file or directory
```

GNU `ls` spells out the `$'\r'`; many tools print a name that looks
exactly right. And a **script** saved with CRLF fails on its first
line, because the shebang now names a program called `bash\r`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "hello"' > crlf.sh
chmod u+x crlf.sh
./crlf.sh
```

```{.console}
/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
```

(The second line is `env` guessing at a different problem; ignore it.
Older `env`, such as Nova's, prints only the first line. Ubuntu 26.04's
`env` writes it as `env: $'bash\r': No such file or directory`; on a
Mac it is `env: bash\r: No such file or directory`. With `#!/bin/bash`
instead, bash 5.1 (Nova) and 5.3 say `/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No
such file or directory`, with status 126 instead of 127: the `^M` is
the carriage return. Bash 5.2 says only `cannot execute: required file
not found`, which is even less helpful.)

**How to detect it.** Look with `cat -A` (for `^M`), and count with
`grep -c $'\r' file`, which prints how many lines contain a carriage
return: `7` for the CSV, `0` for the TSV. Do not rely on `file`: it
reports `with CRLF line terminators` for some text (`file crlf.sh`
does), but once it recognises a CSV it says only `CSV ASCII text`, with
or without carriage returns (Ubuntu's `file` 5.45; macOS's and Nova's
5.39 say `CSV text`). On a two-line CSV saved by Excel, `file` did mention CRLF; on
the seven-line sheet it did not, so its answer depends on the file.

**Now name it.** Linux and macOS end each line with one character, a
**line feed** (LF, `\n`). Windows ends lines with two, **carriage
return + line feed** (CRLF, `\r\n`). CRLF is normal in CSV files, and
proper CSV readers in R and Python handle it (@sec-tabular-data); what
breaks is a shell tool or simple script that keeps the `\r` as part of
the last field. Files get CRLF endings from Windows editors, Excel's
"Save as CSV", and email attachments. In WSL, files under `/mnt/c`
(@sec-orientation's pitfall) are often edited with Windows programs,
which is where the CRLF comes from; the folder itself does not change
the bytes. Excel's **CSV UTF-8** format also puts three invisible bytes,
a **byte order mark**, before the first column name: `cat -A` shows
`M-oM-;M-?sample,reads^M$`, and a shell tool then sees a first column
called something other than `sample`. `sed '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//'`
removes it; R's and Python's CSV readers handle it.

**Fix it** by deleting the `\r` at each line end. Write a fixed copy
first and check it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sed 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv > samples_lf.csv
grep -c $'\r' samples_lf.csv
echo $?
grep -c ',30$' samples_lf.csv
```

```{.console}
0
1
2
```

No carriage returns left, and the count is right. The `1` from `echo
$?` is not a failure: `grep` exits with `1` when it finds no matching
lines, which is what you wanted here (@sec-shell-scripts returns to
this). Once you trust the command, GNU `sed -i 's/\r$//' file` fixes a
file in place: on your own copy, never on `data/raw/`
(@sec-text-tools). Two other tools you will see: `tr -d '\r' < in >
out` deletes **every** carriage return, not only those at line ends
(fine for a sample sheet), and `dos2unix file`, where installed, does
the same job as `sed`. Line-ending fixes are for text files only, never
for compressed or binary data.

: Line endings by system. {#tbl-line-endings}

| System | Line ending | Bytes | `cat -A` shows | Convert with |
|:-------|:------------|:------|:---------------|:-------------|
| Linux, macOS | LF | `\n` | `$` | (already right) |
| Windows | CRLF | `\r\n` | `^M$` | `sed 's/\r$//' in > out` |
| Classic Mac OS (before 2001) | CR | `\r` | one long line with `^M` | `tr '\r' '\n' < in > out` |

Prevent it where you can. VS Code shows `LF` or `CRLF` in the status
bar at the bottom of the window; click it to change a file, and set
`"files.eol": "\n"` in your settings to make LF the default
([VS Code docs](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/codebasics)).
Git can convert line endings for you (@sec-git). Before a pipeline run,
check sample sheets with `grep -c $'\r'` (@sec-nf-core). One more
invisible character from Excel, the byte-order mark at the start of a
file, is @sec-numbers-encodings.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: CRLF from Windows or Excel
Files from Windows or Excel can end lines in CRLF. Shell tools then see
a `\r` stuck to the last field, and matches and comparisons fail
silently. Check with `cat -A` (look for `^M`) or `grep -c $'\r'` before
a script reads them.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "A CSV file is a CSV file; where it was saved doesn't matter"
**Reality.** The program and system that saved it decide its line
endings (and whether it starts with an invisible byte-order mark).
A `\r` at each line end sticks to the last field, so matches and
comparisons on it fail without an error.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `cat -A samples.csv` shows `^M$` at every line end.
Name one way it got that way and one fix.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It was saved by Excel or a Windows editor. Fix: `sed 's/\r$//'
samples.csv > samples_lf.csv`, check with `grep -c $'\r'
samples_lf.csv` (prints `0`), then use the new file.
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-linux-system-summary}

- A permission string is a type letter and three triplets (user, group,
  other) of `r`, `w`, `x`; each triplet is also one octal digit (4 + 2 +
  1). On a folder, `r` lists names, `x` reaches the entries, and `w`
  with `x` adds or removes them, so deleting a file depends on its
  folder. `chmod` changes permissions; read the string and change one
  letter, never `777`.
- A script runs as a command with a shebang line (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`)
  and the `x` bit. `Permission denied` (126) means found but not
  runnable; `command not found` (127) means not on `PATH`.
- Bash checks aliases, functions, and builtins, then searches the `PATH`
  folders in order and runs the first match; `type -a` shows them all.
  `pixi run` and `module load` work by putting a folder first on
  `PATH`.
- `export` passes a variable to the programs a shell starts; a line in
  `~/.bashrc` sets it for every new terminal. Login shells read the
  first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`; in the
  book's setup that file reads `~/.bashrc`. Back up before editing,
  and keep it silent.
- A process has a PID and a parent. {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} and `kill` ask it
  to end, `kill -9` forces it, {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}} only pauses it. `df`
  shows how full a disk is, `du` what is in folders; on a cluster your
  limit is a quota. GNU and BSD tools share names but not options.
  Windows line endings leave a `\r` on the last field: find it with
  `cat -A` or `grep -c $'\r'`, remove it with `sed 's/\r$//'`.

: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-ch07-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Who am I, which groups | `whoami`, `id` |
| Read permissions | `ls -l`, `ls -ld folder`, `stat -c '%A %a %n' f` |
| Change permissions | `chmod u+x f`, `chmod a-w f`, `chmod 644 f`, `chmod 700 d`, `chmod -R g+rX d` |
| Make a script run | `#!/usr/bin/env bash` on line 1, `chmod u+x script.sh`, `./script.sh` |
| What runs, from where | `type -a name`, `echo "$PATH" \| tr ':' '\n'`, `hash -r` |
| Add a folder to `PATH` | `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"` |
| Variables | `NAME=value cmd`, `export NAME=value`, `env`, `locale` |
| Startup files | `~/.bashrc`; `cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07`; `source ~/.bashrc` |
| Processes | `cmd &`, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`, `ps`, `ps -u "$USER"`, `top`, `kill %1`, `kill PID`, `kill -9 PID` |
| Disk | `df -h folder`, `du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h` |
| Which tools | `type -a ls`, `ls --version` |
| Line endings | `cat -A f`, `grep -c $'\r' f`, `sed 's/\r$//' in > out` |

## Exercises {#sec-linux-system-exercises}

Do these in `~/bioinf-computing-ch07`. Exercise 4 is the only one that
changes a file outside it (your `~/.bashrc`, after a backup).

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Make a broken tool run.** A labmate's script,
`count_lines.sh`, prints a file's name and its number of lines. It
arrived from a Windows laptop with a sample sheet. Set up the copy (the
`printf` writes the script with Windows line endings, and `chmod 644`
makes sure it starts out not executable):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' \
  '# count_lines.sh: print a file name and its number of lines' \
  'printf "%s: %s lines\n" "$(basename "$1")" "$(wc -l < "$1")"' \
  > bin/count_lines.sh
chmod 644 bin/count_lines.sh
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv samples.csv
```

The goal: from any folder, `count_lines.sh
~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv` prints `samples.csv: 7 lines`.
Fix one fault at a time, using only the message, and run the script
**by its path** until the last step:

1. Run `./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv`. Fix what the message says.
2. Run the same command again. Fix what the new message says.
3. Run it once more: it should work.
4. `cd ~` and run it **by name**: `count_lines.sh
   ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv`. Make that work for this
   terminal.

Then the sample sheet: count its rows with 30 reads (`grep -c ',30$'`)
and its carriage returns (`grep -c $'\r'`), fix it in place with GNU
`sed -i`, and count again. Record each message and fix in `NOTEBOOK.md`.
(The script's `$1`, `$( )`, and `basename` are @sec-shell-scripts; you
only need to make it run.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
bash: ./bin/count_lines.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines
$ cd ~
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
bash: count_lines.sh: command not found
$ export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin:$PATH"
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines
```

1. No `x` bit (126): `chmod u+x`. 2. Windows line endings in the
shebang, so `env` looked for `bash\r` (127): remove the `\r`. 4. The
folder is not on `PATH` (127): add it, for this terminal only.

The sheet:

```{.console}
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
7
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
2
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
```

The line count was 7 before and after: `wc -l` counts line ends, and a
carriage return does not change how many there are. Only the `\r`
count shows that the fix worked. (`echo $?` after the last `grep` gives
`1`, "no lines matched", which is the result you wanted.)
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Read and set permissions.** In
`~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2/`, make `notes.txt`, `run.sh`, and a
folder `private/`. Set them to `-rw-r--r--`, `-rwxr-xr-x`, and
`drwx------`: once with symbolic `chmod`, then again from the start
with octal. Check with `ls -l` and `stat -c '%A %a %n'`. Then explain,
from `ls -ld ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw`, why `rm` on a raw file
fails.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2 && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2
touch notes.txt run.sh && mkdir private
chmod u+x,go+rx run.sh              # from -rw-r--r--: add x for all, r for group and other
chmod go-rx private                 # from drwxr-xr-x
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt run.sh private
chmod 644 notes.txt && chmod 755 run.sh && chmod 700 private
```

```{.console}
-rw-r--r-- 644 notes.txt
-rwxr-xr-x 755 run.sh
drwx------ 700 private
```

`notes.txt` already had `644` from the umask. `data/raw` is
`dr-xr-xr-x`: nobody has `w` on the folder, and removing a file changes
the folder, so `rm` is refused even with `-f`.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Which copy runs?** Make a fake `seqkit` that only prints
a version, put its folder first on `PATH` in this terminal, and see
which copy each command finds:

