```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)"' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
chmod u+x ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin:$PATH"
type -a seqkit
seqkit version
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash -c 'type -a seqkit; seqkit version'
```

Which copy runs in each case, and why? Close the terminal afterwards to
undo the `PATH` change. (Do not put this in `~/.bashrc`.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v2.14.0
```

In the plain terminal, `fakebin` is first on `PATH`, so bare `seqkit`
is the fake. (If another seqkit is installed on your machine,
`type -a` lists it below.) Under `pixi run`, the environment's folder
goes in front of everything, so the real seqkit wins, and `type -a`
shows the fake one second. This is why the book always writes `pixi
run seqkit`.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Make a setting permanent.** Back up `~/.bashrc` with `cp
-n`, then add `export EDITOR=nano` (and, on a cluster where
@sec-book-setup told you to, the `PIXI_CACHE_DIR` line) if it is not
there yet. Prove it works in a new terminal and, if you have a cluster
account, in a new SSH login. Record in `NOTEBOOK.md` which of
`~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`, and `~/.bashrc` exist
on each machine, and which one reads `~/.bashrc`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07
grep -n 'EDITOR=' ~/.bashrc # <1>
grep -qxF 'export EDITOR=nano' ~/.bashrc ||
  echo 'export EDITOR=nano' >> ~/.bashrc # <2>
ls -a ~ | grep -E '^\.(bash|profile)'
grep -n bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile 2>/dev/null
```
1. Look first. If an active line (not starting with `#`) already sets
   `EDITOR` to something else, change that line in `nano` rather than
   adding a second one.
2. `-x` matches whole lines only, `-F` treats the text as plain text,
   not a pattern, and `-q` prints nothing. The `||` adds the line only
   if that exact line is missing, so running it twice does not add it
   twice. A commented-out `# export EDITOR=vim` does not count.

A later line wins over an earlier one, so the real check is a new
terminal, where `echo "$EDITOR"` prints `nano`. On Ubuntu and WSL you will usually find
`~/.profile` reading `~/.bashrc`; on a Mac, `~/.bash_profile` from
@sec-orientation. If the SSH login does not see the setting, the
cluster's login file does not read `~/.bashrc` (see the check in
@sec-linux-system-startup).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Find and end a process; find the space.** Start `sleep
600 &`, find its PID with `ps` and in `top`, end it with `kill`, and
confirm with `jobs`. Then list the five largest items in
`~/bioinf-computing`, hidden ones included. Which is the environment,
and why is it so large compared with the data?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sleep 600 &
ps
kill %1          # or: kill <the PID from ps>
jobs
cd ~/bioinf-computing
du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5
```

In `top`, look for `sleep` in the `COMMAND` column (press `q` to quit).
The largest item is `.pixi` (about 1.3 GB on Linux): Python, R, and
seqkit with every library they need, for one operating system. The
data are a few megabytes. Real projects have far more data, but
environments are always this kind of size, which is why pixi's cache
and environments go on project storage on a cluster (@sec-book-setup).
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-linux-system-reading}

- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, chapters on permissions,
  processes, the environment, and customising the prompt --- the same
  ground as this chapter, with more examples; free online.
- @ramey2025bash, the [*Bash Reference
  Manual*](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/), sections *Bash
  Startup Files*, *Environment*, and *Job Control* --- the exact rules
  behind @tbl-startup-files and @fig-process-states, short and
  authoritative.
- @gnu2026coreutils, the [GNU coreutils
  manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/), chapter *File
  permissions* --- everything about `chmod`, including setgid, the
  sticky bit, and capital `X`; also `df`, `du`, and `stat`.
- The [Linux man-pages project](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/):
  `signal(7)` for the full list of signals, `environ(7)` for
  environment variables, and `execve(2)` for how the kernel reads a
  shebang line --- for the curious.
